lines.text: Asked for the pH of a strong base → $[\ce{OH^-}]$ from its formula, $[\ce{H^+}] = K_\mathrm{w}/[\ce{OH^-}]$, then $\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\ce{H^+}]$ ({{lesson:6.2}})
Titre given, unknown concentration asked → $n = cV$ for the known solution, use the mole ratio, divide by the unknown's volume ({{lesson:6.3}})

pH of a weak acid from $K_\mathrm{a}$ and $c$ → $[\ce{H^+}] \approx \sqrt{K_\mathrm{a} \times c}$; for a weak base find $[\ce{OH^-}]$ the same way, then $\mathrm{pH} = 14.00 - \mathrm{pOH}$ at 298 K ({{lesson:6.4}})
Choose an indicator for a titration → predict the equivalence-point pH from the salt formed, then pick the indicator whose range includes it ({{lesson:6.5}}, {{lesson:6.6}})
pH of a buffer, or after acid or alkali is added to one → react the addition first in moles, then $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} + \log_{10}\frac{[\ce{A^-}]}{[\ce{HA}]}$ ({{lesson:6.7}})
Asked to balance a redox half-equation in acid → balance the atom that changes oxidation state, then O with $\ce{H2O}$, H with $\ce{H+}$, and charge with $\ce{e-}$ ({{lesson:6.8}})

Asked to identify an electrode or give its sign → name it from the reaction (oxidation = anode, reduction = cathode), then the sign from the cell type: anode $-$ in a voltaic cell, $+$ in an electrolytic cell ({{lesson:6.10}})

Asked for the product of oxidizing an alcohol → classify it first: primary gives an aldehyde (distil off) then a carboxylic acid (reflux, excess oxidizing agent); secondary gives a ketone; tertiary resists oxidation ({{lesson:6.12}})

Asked whether a redox reaction is spontaneous → find the species reduced as written, take its half-cell as the cathode, and use $E^\ominus_\text{cell} = E^\ominus_\text{cathode} - E^\ominus_\text{anode}$; positive means spontaneous under standard conditions ({{lesson:6.13}})

Asked for the products of electrolysing a solution with inert electrodes → compare each ion with water: at the cathode the more positive $E^\ominus$ is reduced (water $\pu{-0.83 V}$), at the anode the less positive is oxidized (water $\pu{+1.23 V}$); concentrated chloride gives chlorine ({{lesson:6.14}})
Asked whether a species is a radical → count its electrons, allowing for charge; an odd total means an unpaired electron ({{lesson:6.15}})

Asked to identify the nucleophile and electrophile → find the species that donates an electron pair (a lone pair or a $\ce{C=C}$ π pair); the species that accepts it is the electrophile ({{lesson:6.16}})
Asked for the charge on a complex ion → charge of the metal ion plus the sum of the ligand charges ({{lesson:6.17}})
Halogenoalkane rate data → rate independent of $[\ce{Nu^-}]$ means SN1, rate $= k[\text{RX}]$; first order in both means SN2, rate $= k[\text{RX}][\ce{Nu^-}]$ ({{lesson:6.18}})
Major product of HX or water adding to an unsymmetrical alkene → compare the two possible carbocations; the more stable one (tertiary > secondary > primary) gives the major product ({{lesson:6.19}})
